title: Counting the Corneal Cells

patient.name: Mdm Lee Bee Hoon
patient.presenting_complaint: Pre-cataract surgery work-up; reports vision is blurrier in the mornings
patient.address: Blk 25 Ang Mo Kio Ave 3, #18-586, Singapore 115238

history.hpc: Mdm Lee is being assessed before cataract surgery and is referred for an endothelial cell count. She says: 'Morning time my vision more blur, afternoon a bit better, why ah?' Vision that is worse in the morning and improves later can suggest corneal endothelial dysfunction (e.g., Fuchs dystrophy). The OT must perform specular microscopy and document the endothelial cell density.
history.pmhx: Bilateral cataracts (for surgery). Possible Fuchs endothelial dystrophy noted by doctor.
history.family_hx: Mother had 'cornea problem' and cataract surgery

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Cornea shows subtle changes (possible guttata); cataract both eyes
examination_findings.fundus: For doctor as part of pre-op assessment

investigations.endothelial_cell_count: Specular microscopy performed for both eyes. Endothelial cell density measured with morphology. Right eye ~1300 cells/mm2, left ~1450 cells/mm2 — below the >2000 normal and under the 1500 concern threshold, with irregular cell shapes consistent with Fuchs endothelial dystrophy. Findings documented for the doctor.
investigations.measurement_quality: Clear specular images obtained; representative central counts taken for both eyes.

diagnosis: Low endothelial cell density (below the 1500 concern level) with irregular morphology, consistent with Fuchs endothelial dystrophy, in a patient due for cataract surgery — important because a low count raises the risk of corneal decompensation after surgery. The OT competency is reliable measurement and clear documentation; the surgical implications are the doctor's to weigh.

immediate: Confirm the indication (pre-cataract assessment, morning blur) and which eyes to measure
Explain the non-contact specular microscopy and position the patient with good fixation
Obtain clear specular images and representative central counts for both eyes
Note the cell density against normal (>2000) and concern (<1500) thresholds, and the morphology
Document diagnosis, indication, RE/LE, and findings (cell density, morphology) for the doctor
Flag the low counts to the doctor as relevant to surgical risk (do not counsel on surgery yourself)
follow_up: Doctor to factor the low endothelial count into the surgical plan and consent (decompensation risk)
Complete the rest of the pre-op assessment
patient_education: Explain the test counts the cells on the back of the cornea that keep it clear
Explain that morning blur can relate to these cells and that the doctor will review the result
Reassure her the scan is quick and painless
Defer detailed surgical implications to the doctor

Notes family/clinical clues suggesting endothelial dystrophy
Explains the procedure to gain cooperation

Obtains representative central counts for both eyes
Interprets density against the >2000 normal and <1500 concern thresholds
Documents diagnosis, indication, RE/LE, density, and morphology
Recognises a low count with irregular morphology as consistent with Fuchs dystrophy
Understands a low endothelial count raises post-surgery decompensation risk
Knows the OT role is measurement/documentation, not surgical counselling
Flags the result appropriately to the doctor
Produces reliable counts and documents density and morphology
Flags the low counts to the doctor as relevant to surgical risk
